ABSTRACT Introduction Although an acute exercise session typically increases bone turnover markers (BTM), the impact of subsequent sessions and the interaction with preexercise calcium intake remain unclear despite the application to the “real-life” training of many competitive athletes. Methods Using a randomized crossover design, elite male rowers ( n = 16) completed two trials, a week apart, consisting of two 90-min rowing ergometer sessions (EX1, EX2) separated by 150 min. Before each trial, participants consumed a high (CAL; ~1000 mg) or isocaloric low (CON; <10 mg) calcium meal. Biochemical markers including parathyroid hormone (PTH), serum ionized calcium (iCa) and BTMs (C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen, osteocalcin) were monitored from baseline to 3 h after EX2. Results Although each session caused perturbances of serum iCa, CAL maintained calcium concentrations above those of CON for most time points, 4.5% and 2.4% higher after EX1 and EX2, respectively. The decrease in iCa in CON was associated with an elevation of blood PTH ( P < 0.05) and C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen ( P < 0.0001) over this period of repeated training sessions and their recovery, particularly during and after EX2. Preexercise intake of calcium-rich foods lowered BTM over the course of a day with several training sessions. Conclusions Preexercise intake of a calcium-rich meal before training sessions undertaken within the same day had a cumulative and prolonged effect on the stabilization of blood iCa during exercise. In turn, this reduced the postexercise PTH response, potentially attenuating the increase in markers of bone resorption. Such practical strategies may be integrated into the athlete’s overall sports nutrition plan, with the potential to safeguard long-term bone health and reduce the risk of bone stress injuries. Key Words ENDURANCE NUTRIENT TIMING OSTEOCALCIN PTH Β-CTX-I CALCIUM BONE OPEN-ACCESS TRUE Athletes often exhibit suboptimal bone health despite the well-known positive effects of exercise on bone ( 1 ). Immediate concerns include the effects of bone stress injuries on training consistency and availability for competition, whereas an increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures may be seen later in an athlete’s career or after retirement ( 2 , 3 ). Such issues are known in a variety of sports such as cycling ( 4 ), dance ( 5 ), and distance running ( 6 ) and are seen among males and females ( 7 ). Key contributors toward bone health include energy availability, weight-bearing/bone loading exercise, and vitamin D ( 1 , 8 ). However, some athletes do consistently optimize these factors, and/or they may still require other measures to adequately support bone health. Therefore, there is interest in addressing other mechanisms by which bone metabolism may be perturbed. Elite rowers typically present with normal areal bone mineral density (aBMD) relative to general population norms; however, this may be inadequate to withstand the load required by the sport ( 9 ) and may be associated with history of bone stress injury of the rib ( 10 ), associated with significant training time loss and performance decrement ( 11 ). A series of studies have identified that acute changes in serum ionized calcium (iCa) was associated with exercise correlate with bone turnover. For example, 2 h of moderate-intensity cycling in male cyclists was associated with a decrease in iCa and an elevation in parathyroid hormone (PTH) ( 12 ), suggesting that bone resorption may have been upregulated in an attempt to stabilize the reduction in iCa. It was hypothesized that increasing absorption of calcium from the gut during exercise, achieved by consuming calcium-rich foods or supplements before or during the session, might prevent bone resorption by providing an alternative calcium source. Indeed, preexercise calcium intake in elite male triathletes ( 13 ), as well as male ( 14 ) and female ( 15 ) cyclists, was found to suppress the cycling-associated rise in PTH and attenuated the increase in C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTX-1), a marker of bone breakdown, in some ( 13 , 15 ), but not all, protocols ( 14 ). The divergent outcomes may be due to differences in the source and timing of calcium intake (>60 vs 20 min prior). Studies in older individuals with lower levels of fitness who undertook brisk walking exercise also show similar responses to calcium support ( 16 – 18 ). These studies provide robust evidence that exercise disrupts calcium homeostasis, likely triggered by a decline in iCa and resulting in an increase in PTH and β-CTX-I. The cause of the perturbation of iCa during exercise and whether this contributes to chronic and clinically meaningful changes in aBMD are still to be determined ( 19 ). The original hypothesis of dermal (sweat) mineral losses ( 20 ) was disproven in two different models. In young adults, there was no difference in exercise-associated iCa changes when brisk walking was undertaken in cool or warm conditions, despite differences in sweat/calcium losses. A more sophisticated methodology, involving the use of an intravenous calcium clamp to maintain iCa allowed more frequent blood sampling, including midexercise samples. Here, a drop in iCa was observed within the first 15 min of a 60-min cycling session at 80% heart rate (HR) maximum, well before significant sweat loss, with the calcium infusion attenuating the increase in PTH and CTX compared with the saline control ( 21 ). Phosphate has also been investigated given its involvement with PTH control at rest and exercise recovery; however, iCa seems more tightly linked with exercise-related PTH changes ( 22 ). To date, studies of these perturbations in iCa and bone metabolism have focused on a single exercise session. However, high-performance athletes typically train multiple times a day, with subsequent sessions frequently commencing within 2–3 h, or before bone responses to the first session have normalized ( 15 ). The acute bone response to repeated exercise sessions has been briefly studied. Scott et al. ( 23 ) investigated the effect of the recovery period (3 vs 23 h) between two bouts of running on bone metabolism, before and during exercise on the trial days and for the following 4 d. Reducing the recovery time from 23 to 3 h did not alter the iCa, PTH, or β-CTX-I response to the second exercise bout or affect P1NP, a marker of bone formation that generally has a more chronic response to stimulus. In contrast, a very short recovery window (40 min) showed a blunting of the PTH response by the rest period ( 24 ). The response to preexercise calcium over multiple sessions has not yet been examined. Together, these studies indicate a perturbation in bone turnover in response to exercise, likely triggered by a decline in iCa, resulting in a PTH-mediated increase in bone resorption. It occurs in a range of ages and fitness levels, between sexes, and in different modes and intensities of exercise. Preexercise calcium intake may maintain iCa and attenuate markers of bone resorption during and after the exercise session. Given the importance of deciphering the real-life significance of preexercise calcium supplementation, this study examined the effect of multiple sessions of exercise in a day (i.e., a typical training day for a high-performance athlete) bone turnover marker (BTM) in elite male rowers, using dietary opportunities to provide preexercise calcium supplementation.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of acute preexercise calcium intake on bone turnover markers and calcium homeostasis in elite male rowers during a day with multiple strenuous, non-weight-bearing training sessions. The findings indicate that consuming a calcium-rich meal before training stabilizes ionized calcium levels, reduces the postexercise parathyroid hormone response, and attenuates the increase in bone resorption markers (e.g., β-CTX-I) over a sustained 7-hour period, thereby supporting long-term bone health and reducing the risk of bone stress injuries.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary calcium supplementation (via whole foods/meals) in conjunction with repeated, strenuous, non-weight-bearing rowing exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Elite male rowers (n=16) participated in two trials, one week apart, each involving two 90-min rowing ergometer sessions (EX1, EX2) separated by 150 minutes. Before each trial, participants consumed either a high calcium meal (~1000 mg, CAL) or an isocaloric low calcium meal (<10 mg, CON). Each exercise session consisted of three 30-minute sets at 90-100% of individual 2 mmol·L−1 capillary blood lactate power (mean 255-260W). Calcium was provided acutely before training sessions. No dose-response comparisons were reported beyond the high versus low intake, nor for exercise intensity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated in the low calcium (CON) group (P < 0.05), with an apparent accentuation after EX2. Concentrations were consistently higher in CON than CAL (P < 0.001) for all time points after the start of EX1 (except 1h post). The high calcium (CAL) group maintained baseline levels, showing a reduced postexercise response with lower PTH adj concentrations over a sustained ~7h period.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulates blood calcium and phosphate levels, primarily by increasing blood calcium through bone resorption and kidney reabsorption, mediating acute bone resorption.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During repeated, strenuous (two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min) non-weight-bearing rowing ergometer exercise, comparing high (~1000 mg) versus low (<10 mg) preexercise calcium meal intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated PTH indicates a physiological response to maintain calcium homeostasis by stimulating bone resorption, potentially contributing to bone stress injuries and suboptimal long-term bone health. Reduced PTH response (attenuated by calcium intake) indicates protection against this mechanism, supporting bone integrity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In the low calcium (CON) group, iCa decreased with each exercise session, being ~4.5% and 2.4% lower than CAL after EX1 and EX2, respectively. The high calcium (CAL) intake maintained iCa concentrations above CON for ~7 hours, spanning the exercise and recovery periods (P < 0.001 for CAL vs CON, also for adjusted iCa).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential for muscle contraction, nerve transmission, hormone secretion, and bone mineralization, playing a critical role in maintaining overall calcium homeostasis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During repeated, strenuous (two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min) non-weight-bearing rowing ergometer exercise, comparing high (~1000 mg) versus low (<10 mg) preexercise calcium meal intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreased iCa indicates a disruption in calcium homeostasis, triggering PTH release and bone resorption. Maintaining iCa levels through preexercise calcium intake stabilizes conditions, supporting musculoskeletal and physiological function, and safeguarding long-term bone health.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (β-CTX-I)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Bone Resorption Marker, electrochemiluminescence immunoassay)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated (P < 0.0001) in the low calcium (CON) group, particularly during and after EX2, with levels being higher than CAL (P < 0.001) from post-EX1 until 2 hours after EX2. The high calcium (CAL) intake maintained β-CTX-I adj at baseline levels, showing no significant increase or only minor, transient elevation over a 6-7 hour period, effectively attenuating exercise-induced increases in bone resorption.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A biochemical marker of bone resorption, indicating the rate of bone breakdown and released from osteoclasts during the breakdown of collagen fibrils.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During repeated, strenuous (two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min) non-weight-bearing rowing ergometer exercise, comparing high (~1000 mg) versus low (<10 mg) preexercise calcium meal intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated β-CTX-I indicates increased bone breakdown, negatively impacting long-term bone health and increasing bone stress injury risk. Attenuating this increase through preexercise calcium intake supports bone integrity and reduces bone loss.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Bone Formation Marker, automated chemiluminescent immunoassay)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Unaffected by preexercise calcium intake. Decreased significantly after feeding (P < 0.0001), increased during EX2 (P < 0.001), and decreased during recovery from both sessions (P < 0.05 for EX1, P < 0.001 for EX2).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A protein primarily synthesized by osteoblasts, reflecting bone formation (synthesis of bone matrix).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During repeated, strenuous (two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min) rowing ergometer exercise, after feeding, and during recovery periods, with high (~1000 mg) versus low (<10 mg) preexercise calcium meal intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects bone formation activity in response to exercise and feeding. Acute preexercise calcium intake did not significantly influence total osteocalcin levels, suggesting it's more influenced by energy/carbohydrate availability during exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Bone Formation Marker, automated chemiluminescent immunoassay)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Unaffected by preexercise calcium intake. Showed small but significant increases associated with each exercise bout, with levels highest during the recovery period from EX2 (P < 0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A form of osteocalcin reflecting bone formation, with potential endocrine effects related to energy metabolism and bone quality.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During repeated, strenuous (two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min) rowing ergometer exercise and recovery periods, with high (~1000 mg) versus low (<10 mg) preexercise calcium meal intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects bone formation activity. Acute preexercise calcium intake did not significantly influence ucOC levels, suggesting it's more influenced by energy/carbohydrate availability during exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Unaffected by preexercise calcium intake. Showed a minor increase from pre-EX1 to post-EX2 (P < 0.01 and P < 0.05 for immediately and 1 h post, respectively).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Ratio indicating the carboxylation status of osteocalcin, reflecting vitamin K status and potentially bone quality or metabolic activity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During repeated, strenuous (two 90-min sessions separated by 150 min) rowing ergometer exercise and recovery periods, with high (~1000 mg) versus low (<10 mg) preexercise calcium meal intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects the balance between uncarboxylated and total osteocalcin, which could indicate bone matrix quality or metabolic signaling, with no acute effect observed from preexercise calcium intake, suggesting other factors were more influential.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels were insufficient in 30% of the study sample.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of vitamin D status, essential for calcium absorption, bone mineralization, and immune function; deficiency can secondarily affect PTH levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: General health status of elite male rowers during the study, coinciding with an annual seasonal nadir for vitamin D levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Insufficient levels highlight a common nutritional concern in athletes; however, due to the crossover design and absence of frank deficiency, it was deemed unlikely to have affected the main study findings related to acute calcium intervention.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Marginally elevated; noted as the only abnormality in the study cohort.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A stress hormone involved in regulating metabolism, immune response, and stress response; if chronically elevated, it may contribute to bone loss.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: General health status of the study cohort, assessed after a short break in the training season. Assessment in elite male rowers undergoing high or low calcium dietary interventions and intense rowing exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Ongoing elevated cortisol may contribute toward bone loss, independent of low energy availability. The marginal elevation was noted as an abnormality in the cohort, but not directly linked to the calcium intervention effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Approximately 1.8% higher in CON than CAL (P < 0.001). Increased by ~2.3% from baseline at the end of EX1, then decreased by 7.8% during recovery. Generally increased during exercise and decreased during recovery in both conditions.
